questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to stay within Europe and go to a university, which UCPH already had an agreement with, to make the planning easier. It was also important to me that there was a wide range courses available in English, which seemed interesting and relevant to me. And I had already been to Italy several times before, so I knew I would like the place and culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The information before my stay was very lackluster, so the practical parts consisted more of guesswork than guidance.
But after getting used to their way, the duration of the exchange itself was enjoyable enough. I liked the classes and professors I had, and got to experience something different from what I'm used to.
Unfortunately, their rules for exams are not as suited for exchange students, as I had to take 8 exams over two months, while staying there for longer or permanently allows you to space them out over a year. I found this take up more of my time, than I would have wished for, and resulted in not getting to travel as much around the country as I had planned on.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
I had to find almost all information myself, looking through their website and different portals, sometimes with outdated information and dates.
The exchange office was out of office for almost all of August, and when we started receiving the first information in September, we were asked not to contact them with any questions apart from cancellation of our exchange etc. 
This meant that it was hard to know when the classes and intro days started, and thus when to book flights and accommodation etc.
I was also assigned to a different faculty than the one I wanted to take my courses at, which meant that (even after asking to be moved to the correct one without success) I couldn't get access to the pages with information on my courses, such as course material, or that the start of a certain class had been postponed a week.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: An intro day was held by the Erasmus Student Network, which was nice, but was more regarding their offers (bars/restaurants, sports days, city tours etc.) than practical information. Mot much assistance was given by the university itself, apart from finally getting information on course registration and such after classes had begun.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
As I didn't receive any official information on, when the classes would begin (which was the last week of September in my case), I waited a long time with booking my accommodation. At this point not much was available, and I had to stay at different places to get accommodation for the whole duration of my stay. It also ended up being quite expensive.
But there seemed to be a lot of furnished apartment to rent in the city, which maybe would've been available in that period, had I looked earlier.

Also, the host institution did seem to offer some type of housing, but ticking off the option to accept it in their application form didn't seem to have any effect.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It probably depends on how long before your stay you are looking, but in the months up to the start of the semester, most available accommodations are either far from campus (40-60 minutes), very expensive or both.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You have to sign up for an intranet called Unimia, where you can sign up for the courses you want. You also don't pick the courses from a list like at UCPH, but simply by typing them out. This, combined with the fact that you don't get any confirmation that you actually have been registered, gave me a lot of doubts on whether that was the actual registration. But it turned out to be the right way.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The email with the instructions arrived after the courses had begun. Searching through the website and hoping that I was doing the correct thing, was what got me through it.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was admitted to all of the courses I registered for, despite not getting any confirmation or declination, as mentioned.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Have a lot of patience with the information and trust that you are doing it right.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I only took master's courses, as they were available in English, but I found the difficulty to be very similar to what I'm used to. Some parts were more difficult and other easier, depending on how much I knew about the topics beforehand - but that is hard to avoid.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I had a few practical and theoretical/computational exercises in a few of my courses, but otherwise it was solely lectures. I definitely missed the problem solving, which I am used to have at UCPH. You were also not expected to buy/read books for the courses, but the professors often still had recommendations.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Cell therapy and gene silencing
- Molecular pharmacology and immunology
- Communicable and non-communicable disease
- Biomarkers: From identification to exploitation

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I specifically liked the course "Cell therapy and gene silencing". It had a practical laboratory exercise and a theoretical on CRISPR, which I found to be a very nice change of pace. The subjects discussed during the lectures were also interesting to me and tied well in together with my previous courses in Copenhagen.

questions.answer: Accommodation ended up being very expensive for me, but otherwise I don't think anything surprised me.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transportation within Milano is very affordable in comparison to Copenhagen

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There seemed to be a lot of opportunities from bars to trips to nearby cities. I think I only attended the intro day and a city tour, but the city tour was nice.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: City tour, restaurants/bars/clubs, trips to other cities, sports day, museum trips etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: As mentioned, I only attended the city tour, and I would recommend it. It was a nice way to see the different areas and buildings and hear about the history behind them.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Exploring the city or other cities, though be prepared for a lot of people in the central part of Milano - especially on days off. In my experience trips taking up your whole weekend are better placed within the first two months of your exchange, before the exams begins.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: For me, it took a week or two to get used to the culture. When not in the area of the campus, most people don't speak English, so being prepared for that and picking up a few Italian words is very helpful.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Some of my classes barely had any international students and already knew each other from past semesters, which made it harder to socialize, than in some of my classes, where nobody knew each other. But everyone I met was very friendly, and I was also invited to cafés/restaurants and parties, so I would recommend just being open meeting new people. And attending the Erasmus event's will obviously also help meeting new people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: In the beginning, it felt a little weird not being able to speak to people, when we didn't share a common language. But after a while I picked up some phrases and got more used to finding other ways to communicate.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: A lot of people being very friendly and helpful.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Don't expect the practical part of registration and getting information to be easy, but trust that it will work out.
- Even though it might be overwhelming when still feeling like you are settling in, the beginning of your exchange might be the best time to go on trip to other cities (due to exams in Dec-Feb).
- Be open-minded: A lot of things are done differently regarding course structure, exams etc.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The campus is spread out across a big part of the city, so it can be a good idea to check where your different classes are located, when choosing them. But be prepared that the location given on their page is not always accurate, and it might take some time to find the first time.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Challenging myself by living in a different country and getting used to a different educational system and culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Just being away from most of the things in your life, you are used to, in general. Finding new ways to make things work.
And of course the various challenges with course registration and faculty assignment, as mentioned throughout my travel report.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
